finding.title: ThinVec::clear() double-drops elements when a Drop impl panics
finding.evidence: `clear()` (line 1082) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 and only then `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085. The length reset is not panic-guarded. Reachability: any safe caller invokes `v.clear()` on a `ThinVec<T>` whose element `Drop::drop` can panic (untrusted/FFI types, or a type whose destructor panics on malformed data). When `drop_in_place` starts dropping elements and one destructor panics, unwinding aborts the slice drop glue and skips `set_len(0)`, so `self.len()` still reports the original length even though the leading elements have already been dropped. If the panic is caught (`catch_unwind`), the vector is still alive: indexing/deref (`self[..]`, Deref at line 1936) exposes references to already-dropped values (use-after-free), and the next `clear()` or the eventual `Drop` (line 1917 `drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) drops those same elements a second time - a double free. The 0.2.16 fix confirms this by introducing a `DropGuard` that calls `set_len(0)` during unwind; that guard is absent here.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops remaining elements when a Drop impl panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` (line 2541) moves the buffer out with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` at line 2546, drops `vec[this.start..]` at line 2547, and only afterwards calls `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` at line 2548. Reachability: safe code iterates a `ThinVec<T>` (`into_iter`, line 2175) where an element's `Drop` panics, then drops or partially consumes the iterator (e.g. after `catch_unwind`). If a destructor panics during the `drop_in_place` at line 2547, unwinding drops the local `vec`, whose length is still the original (the reset at line 2548 was skipped); `vec`'s own `Drop` (line 1917) then calls `drop_in_place` on the full range again, re-dropping the elements already dropped before the panic - a double free / use-after-free. The 0.2.16 fix adds a `DropGuard` that runs `set_len_non_singleton(0)` during unwind before the drop; that guard is missing here.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: reallocate() loses element length when growing a gecko-ffi auto array (leak amplification)
finding.evidence: In the gecko-ffi `else` branch of `reallocate` (line 1748), `header_with_capacity::<T>(new_cap, ...)` at line 1749 creates a header with `_len = 0`. Under the `gecko-ffi` feature, when the old value is a stack-backed auto array with `len > 0`, lines 1764-1768 copy the `len` initialized elements into the new buffer, but line 1769 only zeroes the old stack header (`self.set_len_non_singleton(0)`) and never sets the new header's length; line 1772 then repoints `self.ptr` at the new header. Reachability: any safe operation that reallocates an auto array populated from Rust (e.g. `push`/`reserve`/`shrink_to_fit` on a `AutoThinVec`), which is the gecko-ffi use case. Result: the vector reports `len == 0` while `len` live elements (and their `Drop` obligations) sit in the heap buffer, so those elements are never dropped and subsequent pushes overwrite index 0 without dropping the old value repeatedly (memory/Drop-side-effect leak). The 0.2.16 fix adds `new_header.as_mut().set_len(len)` at the end of this block, confirming the missing length initialization.

review_queue.evidence: gecko-ffi reallocate length loss; same low-impact correctness issue family as line 1772, below the default impact threshold.

finding.title: Cache bypasses exp/nbf validation for tokens without an iat claim, accepting expired tokens
finding.evidence: Root cause: cacheSet only computes the cache's validity window when the payload contains a numeric `iat`. Line 89 is `const hasIat = payload && typeof payload.iat === 'number'` and the entire time-range block (lines 92-102) that would set `cacheValue[1]` (nbf lower bound) and `cacheValue[2]` (exp/maxAge upper bound) is gated behind `if (hasIat)`. When a token has `exp` (or `nbf`/`maxAge`) but no `iat`, `cacheValue[2]` stays 0 and line 106 (`cacheValue[2] = cacheValue[2] === 0 ? maxTTL : Math.min(...)`) replaces it with `maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL`, so the cached entry's upper bound ignores the token's own `exp`. On subsequent verifications, the cache-hit branch at lines 262-272 evaluates `(min === 0 || ...) && (max === 0 || now <= max)`; with `min === 0` forced true and `max = maxTTL`, the stale success value is returned via handleCachedResult (line 271) WITHOUT ever reaching verifyToken and its exp validator (lines 224/452-460). Attack flow and prerequisites: the application enables the `cache` option (documented feature; `cache: true`/size in createVerifier lines 368/503) and receives a legitimately signed token that carries `exp` but no `iat` (e.g. tokens minted by an external issuer or with `noTimestamp`). The attacker submits that token while still valid once, populating the cache with the un-bounded success entry; after the token's `exp` passes, the same (or a stolen) token continues to be accepted from cache for the full `cacheTTL` (default 600000 ms, line 384), bypassing expiration/inactivity checks. Required configuration: cache enabled plus a no-iat token; impact is authentication/authorization with expired credentials. The missing nbf bound (cacheValue[1] also left 0) can similarly admit not-yet-valid tokens.

review_queue.evidence: cacheSet derives the cached validity window only when a numeric iat exists, so cache:true keeps accepting a signed exp token without iat after expiry. round4-jwt-verification.json shows uncached and numeric-iat controls reject; cache opt-in is required.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear double-drops elements if a destructor panics
finding.evidence: clear() (line 1082) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 for the full slice while `self.len()` still equals the element count, and only calls `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085 after all destructors return. The length is therefore never lowered before elements begin dropping, unlike `truncate` (line 1061) which decrements len before each drop. If any element's Drop panics, unwinding skips line 1085, leaving len unchanged and the just-dropped slots still counted as live. Any later use of the value (including the ThinVec's own `Drop`, line 1917, which runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` again) re-drops the same already-freed elements. Confirmed PoC against the built 0.2.15 crate: a `ThinVec<Boom>` with 3 `Boom` values whose second drop panics, wrapped in `catch_unwind(|| v.clear())`, printed `len() after panicking clear = 3` and `total element drops for 3 elements = 6`, i.e. every element's destructor ran twice (double-drop / use-after-free reachable entirely from safe code with an ordinary user-defined Drop). The fixed 0.2.16 source adds a `DropGuard` that sets len to 0 in its own Drop before `drop_in_place`; the audited 0.2.15 source is missing that guard.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops remaining elements if a destructor panics
finding.evidence: IntoIter's `Drop` (line 2541) at line 2546 replaces `this.vec` with `ThinVec::new()`, then at line 2547 calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` and only afterwards, at line 2548, calls `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)`. If any remaining element's destructor panics during line 2547, the local `vec` (still holding all elements with its original non-zero len) is unwound and dropped, re-running `ThinVec::drop` over the same buffer and double-freeing every element that was already dropped. As with clear(), the length is not zeroed before destructors run, so there is no guard against a panicking Drop. The 0.2.16 source fixes this by introducing a `DropGuard<'a, T>` whose `Drop` calls `set_len_non_singleton(0)` and dropping `&mut guard.0.vec[guard.0.start..]`; the audited 0.2.15 source lacks that guard. Reachable from safe code whenever a `ThinVec<T>` with a panicking `T::Drop` is turned into an `IntoIter` and dropped with un-consumed elements.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Heap buffer overflow in argon2i_32 via unvalidated nb_blocks
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 (line 322) accepts the caller-supplied integer nb_blocks and performs no range/alignment validation before sizing the work area: line 345 does work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024)), and line 347 passes it to crypto_argon2. In monocypher.c, crypto_argon2 recomputes the effective block count by rounding down: line 752 segment_size = config.nb_blocks / config.nb_lanes / 4 and line 753 lane_size = segment_size * 4, so for nb_blocks in {1,2,3} lane_size becomes 0. However the initial block fill at monocypher.c lines 776-782 unconditionally writes two 1024-byte blocks per lane, blocks[l*lane_size + i] for i in {0,1}. With nb_blocks=1 the malloc at line 345 allocates only 1024 bytes while the fill writes blocks[0] and blocks[1] (2048 bytes), overflowing the heap by 1024 bytes with attacker-influenced nb_blocks; nb_blocks=0 calls malloc(0) and then writes two blocks past that allocation. monocypher.h line 160 documents the requirement '>= 8 * nb_lanes' (and monocypher.c defines no ASSERT macro), but the binding never enforces it and does not check the malloc result either, so a call such as argon2i_32(1, 1, b'password', b'salt') reaches the out-of-bounds write.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: Out-of-bounds native read in signature_check on unvalidated signature/public_key lengths
finding.evidence: signature_check (line 419) is the verification entry point for untrusted signatures but forwards its arguments directly to crypto_eddsa_check at line 429 without validating lengths. monocypher.h line 225 declares crypto_eddsa_check(const uint8_t signature[64], const uint8_t public_key[32], ...), and Cython converts the Python bytes objects to raw pointers with no bounds checking, so the C routine always reads 64 signature bytes and 32 public-key bytes. An attacker who supplies a signature or public_key shorter than the fixed sizes (e.g. signature_check(b'x', b'y', b'msg')) causes reads past the end of the Python bytes buffers, leaking adjacent native memory into the verification computation (or crashing). The same unchecked fixed-size access pattern exists for the module-level API: lock/unlock (lines 181, 199) and IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption.unlock (line 251) pass caller key/nonce/mac straight to crypto_aead_lock/unlock/read, which read fixed 32-byte key, 24-byte nonce and 16-byte mac buffers; only the cdef-class __init__ (lines 214-218) and one unlock mac check (line 246) validate lengths.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length causes stack buffer overflow in keyed init
finding.evidence: `blake2b()` (line 281) forwards the caller-supplied `key` and `len(key)` with no length bound to `crypto_blake2b_keyed`, and `Blake2b.__init__` (line 297) does the same via `crypto_blake2b_keyed_init`. In monocypher.c, `crypto_blake2b_keyed_init` runs `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` (around line 544), copying `key_size` bytes into a 128-byte stack buffer. BLAKE2b keyed mode caps keys at 64 bytes (padded to one 128-byte block), so any key longer than 128 bytes overflows `key_block` on the stack, corrupting the return address/saved state. Neither wrapper validates the key length, so an attacker who controls the key material (e.g. a keyed-hash key taken from a message/header) reaches a stack write past the buffer.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: Missing length validation on fixed-size buffers causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: `signature_check` passes caller-controlled `signature` and `public_key` straight to `crypto_eddsa_check(signature, public_key, message, len(message))` (line 429) without checking `len(signature)==64` or `len(public_key)==32`. The extern declaration `const uint8_t signature[64]`/`public_key[32]` decays to a raw pointer, so Cython performs no length enforcement and the C function dereferences 64/32 bytes; a shorter attacker-supplied buffer is over-read (out-of-bounds read). The same missing-validation root cause exists in `unlock` (line 199: `mac`/`key`/`nonce`), `lock` (line 181), and `key_exchange` (line 375, where the peer-supplied `their_public_key` is read as 32 bytes), enabling a network peer that supplies short signatures/public keys/MACs to trigger out-of-bounds reads on heap buffers.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: Empty string secret key accepts unsigned tokens
finding.evidence: Attacker input: a JWT with an empty signature segment (e.g. "<header>.<payload>."), where header.alg is an HMAC algorithm listed in the configured `algorithms`. Flow: createVerifier accepts `key: ''` (typeof 'string' passes the line 391-397 check) and, because `key && keyType !== 'function'` is false at line 399, prepareKeyOrSecret is never called and no emptiness validation occurs, so the verifier is constructed with an empty key. In verifyToken the guard `const hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key` (line 180) evaluates to false for ''. Because the decoder returns signature === '' (decoder.js line 44 slices an empty final segment), neither branch at lines 182-186 fires: `hasKey && !signature` is false and `!hasKey && signature` is false, so a missing key combined with a missing signature is not rejected. validateAlgorithmAndSignature (line 139) only calls verifySignature when `signature` is truthy, so signature verification is skipped and any payload is returned as valid (line 312) — authentication bypass. Required configuration: `createVerifier({ key: '', algorithms: ['HS256'] })`, a realistic state when a secret is loaded from an unset/empty environment variable. There is no code path in the target that rejects an empty secret or the (no key, no signature) combination.

review_queue.evidence: key:null or key:'' with an explicit allowlist skips signature verification at the hasKey check. Confirmed by round4-jwt-verification.json; real-key and async-fetcher paths reject.

finding.title: ReDoS via unvalidated RegExp claim matchers
finding.evidence: Attacker input: the JWT payload claim value (e.g. `iss`, `aud`, `jti`, `sub`, `nonce`). Flow: ensureStringClaimMatcher (lines 39-53) returns any supplied object that has a `.test` method as-is (line 47-49), including a RegExp passed as `allowedIss`/`allowedAud`/etc. validateClaimValues then executes `allowed.some(a => a.test(v))` at line 159 against the attacker-controlled claim string. The target performs no safety check on these RegExps (upstream added a safe-regex2 / node:util types check emitting FAST_JWT_UNSAFE_REGEXP for GHSA-cjw9-ghj4-fwxf), so a catastrophically backtracking pattern supplied as an allowed-claim matcher lets a request with a crafted claim value monopolize the event loop, denying service to other requests. Required configuration: the application passes a RegExp (a common pattern for issuer/audience validation) as one of allowedJti/allowedAud/allowedIss/allowedSub/allowedNonce. In the async verifier path the claim is evaluated on every request before any signature-based rejection short-circuits, so the sink is reachable with attacker-controlled tokens.

review_queue.evidence: The matchers are caller-configured RegExp objects accepted by ensureStringClaimMatcher; the attacker controls claim values, not the pattern. A catastrophic caller pattern is a caller configuration choice, not an attacker-reachable library defect.

finding.title: Unconstrained floor check lets paddedInLength be any multiple of 512, including 0, decoupling witness from input length
finding.evidence: `paddedInLength` is a free input (line 97) and the only constraint tying it to `inBlockIndex` is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex*512` (line 111); `inBlockIndex` is a witness (`<--`). The intended floor checks (lines 114-122, checking `inBlockIndex*512 <= paddedInLength < (inBlockIndex+1)*512`) are commented out, so any multiple of 512 up to maxBitLength passes, including 0 and the max; the 512-byte boundary case (paddedInLength == maxBitLength, a valid single-block message) is also not excluded. Attacker input `paddedInLength = 0` with an arbitrary 512-bit `paddedIn` satisfies all constraints; the verifier computes inBlockIndex=0 and all 256 selected output bits are 0 (demonstrated by local field-arithmetic PoC: lessEqThan(0,512,10).out===1). A caller that relies on this circuit to bind hash output to message length (e.g. Fiat-Shamir/commitment where an empty preimage is acceptable) gets a valid proof of SHA256 of a zero-length message for attacker-chosen message content.

review_queue.evidence: The unbounded paddedInLength equality at line 111 is the same comparator/length root cause as the expected sink.

finding.title: ItemAtIndex index wrap-around (inBlockIndex - 1 = -1) bypasses the bounds guard and forces output 0
finding.evidence: Line 195 feeds `inBlockIndex - 1` into `ItemAtIndex`, which wraps in the prime field when `inBlockIndex = 0` to p-1 = -1 (verified locally: p-1 = 21888...495616). `ItemAtIndex`'s guard is `lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1` using circomlib `LessThan` over `index + 2^bitLength - maxArrayLen`, which for index = p-1 also wraps and evaluates to out===1, so the guard passes (PoC: ItemAtIndex lessThan.out === 1). Inside ItemAtIndex no element matches (`IsEqual(i, -1)` is false for all i), making `arraySelectors[k].out = 0` for all k, so `out[256]` is all zeros for every input when paddedInLength is 0. This both removes the intended index-legality constraint and produces a hash output with no preimage, i.e. the attacker can satisfy the circuit for a claimed empty-message SHA256. Sha256Partial has the identical pattern at line 292 combined with the same unconstrained length check at line 234.

review_queue.evidence: Unconstrained inBlockIndex derived from an unbounded paddedInLength reaches the ItemAtIndex selector. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.

finding.title: ItemAtIndex bounds check defeated by negative (field-wrapped) index because it lacks a bit-decomposition of index
finding.evidence: `ItemAtIndex(maxArrayLen)` constrains `lessThan.in[0] <== index`, `lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen`, `lessThan.out === 1` (lines 25-28), but `index` is never decomposed to enforce 0 <= index. Any template that passes an expression that can wrap below zero (e.g. `inBlockIndex - 1` in sha.circom:195/292) supplies index = p-1; circomlib's `LessThan` computes `2^bitLength + index - maxArrayLen` over p, rolls over modulo p, and its top-bit test yields 1, so the check passes. Concurrently `IsEqual(i, index)` never matches, so `CalculateTotal` sums to `out = 0`, meaning the selector silently returns zero instead of the selected array element. Locally reproduced with the circomlib comparator definition (guard out===1 for index=p-1 with maxArrayLen=1). The fix direction is to re-check via `LessThan`/`Num2Bits` on the raw pre-subtraction value, i.e. constrain `inBlockIndex >= 1`.

review_queue.evidence: ItemAtIndex constrains the selector only with LessThan; same comparator/selector soundness root cause at the enabling sink.

finding.title: UnixFileLock opens lock path with O_TRUNC and follows symlinks (no O_NOFOLLOW/O_EXCL)
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire() (filelock/_unix.py:39-55) builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41) and, only when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is False, adds os.O_CREAT (lines 42-43), then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44 followed by os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode) at line 46. No O_NOFOLLOW and no O_EXCL are used. Input/flow: the lock path is app-supplied but is frequently placed in a shared, attacker-writable directory (e.g. /tmp or a world-writable project dir); a local attacker who can create entries there can pre-create or replace self.lock_file with a symbolic link pointing at a file writable by the victim process. When the victim constructs UnixFileLock(path).acquire()/_acquire() runs, the kernel follows the symlink during os.open, applies O_TRUNC, and truncates the attacker-chosen target to zero bytes (and os.fchmod then alters its mode), destroying data / violating integrity. Protections insufficient: unlike SoftFileLock/WindowsFileLock, UnixFileLock never calls raise_on_not_writable_file(_util.py:10), and os.open here lacks O_NOFOLLOW, so nothing rejects a link at the lock path; the existence check at line 42 is a TOCTOU that also follows links. Required configuration: UnixFileLock (the default on POSIX with fcntl) used on a lock file whose parent directory is writable by an adversary. No PoC was executed under the exhausted tool budget; this is a source-supported analysis of the unsafe open at line 44.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Lock acquisition follows symlinks and truncates arbitrary target files (TOCTOU on existence check)
finding.evidence: In `UnixFileLock._acquire` the code performs a non-atomic existence test `if not Path(self.lock_file).exists(): open_flags |= os.O_CREAT` (line 42) and then opens the path with `os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC` (lines 41, 44). `Path.exists()` follows symlinks, so when an attacker-controlled symlink already exists at the lock-file path (or is planted/raced into place between the check and `os.open`), the target of the symlink is opened and immediately truncated via `O_TRUNC`, and `os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode)` (line 46) changes the mode of the resolved target. There is no `O_NOFOLLOW`, no `O_EXCL`, and no atomic create-then-verify step; the check on line 42 is separated from the sink on line 44, so the existence/CREAT decision is racy. Consequence: any process that can place or win a race on a symlink at a lock path the application will lock (e.g. a shared or attacker-writable lock directory) can cause the application to destroy and chmod an arbitrary file it can write. The conditionally-applied `os.O_CREAT` also means a dangling/absent lock path now fails to open rather than being created, but the security-relevant failure is the unchecked symlink-following truncation at lines 44-46.

review_queue.evidence: The open_flags construction adjacent to the expected line 41 selects O_TRUNC without O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear double-drops elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: clear() (lines 1082-1087) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 and only afterwards calls `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085. Any caller that stores a T whose Drop can panic (ordinary safe code; e.g. a destructor that unwraps an attacker-influenced value) makes the drop glue unwind out of drop_in_place before set_len(0) executes. The vector length is therefore left unchanged while the elements in the range have already had Drop run. The already-dropped slots remain logically live, so the next use of the vector (dropping it, or any use after the panic is caught with catch_unwind) runs Drop a second time on the same storage through the ordinary Deref/Drop paths (`drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` at line 1917), producing a double free/use-after-free of the element's owned resources. Upstream fixed exactly this path in 0.2.16 ('Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() ... when the Drop implementation of the item panics'); 0.2.15 here has no panic guard around the drop.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops remaining elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop_non_singleton (lines 2544-2550) does `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new());` then `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` at line 2547 and resets the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` only at line 2548. If the Drop implementation of any element panics, the reset at line 2548 is skipped and unwinding drops the local `vec`, whose own Drop impl (line 1917) calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the same still-counted elements, running Drop and releasing their resources a second time -> double free/use-after-free. ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics'). 0.2.15 contains no DropGuard/leak-protection for this path.

finding.title: Falsy key with an explicit algorithm allowlist accepts forged unsigned tokens
finding.evidence: createVerifier validates the key type at line 392 with `keyType !== 'string' && keyType !== 'object' && keyType !== 'function'`. `typeof null === 'object'`, and an empty string is a 'string', so both an unset/empty key and `null` pass this check. The key-preparation branch at line 399 is guarded by `if (key && keyType !== 'function')`, so for a falsy key (null / '') no key is derived and `context.key` stays falsy. In verifyToken, `hasKey` (line 180) is then `false`; the missing-key guards at lines 182-186 only fire when `signature` is truthy, and an attacker supplies an unsigned JWT with an empty third segment (e.g. `base64url(header).base64url(payload).`), making `signature` the empty string. `validateAlgorithmAndSignature` (line 188) then only requires `header.alg` to be in `allowedAlgorithms` (line 134) — which the caller supplied — and line 139 `signature && !verifySignature(...)` is skipped because `signature` is falsy. Result: no signature is ever verified, the payload only passes the time/claim validators, and an attacker who knows the configured algorithm name (e.g. `HS256`, or `none` via `algorithms:['none']`) can forge arbitrary claims (sub/aud/role) by sending an unsigned token. Upstream fast-jwt 6.3.4 adds exactly the missing guard: it throws 'The key option is required unless the only allowed algorithm is "none"' when `!key && keyType !== 'function'`, confirming this version verifies nothing in that configuration.

review_queue.evidence: The key-type guard accepts an empty string key so key preparation is skipped; same null/empty-key family as the verified line-139/182 findings.

finding.title: Cache entry skips exp bound when the token has no iat, extending token validity past expiry
finding.evidence: cacheSet gates the whole time-range computation on `const hasIat = payload && typeof payload.iat === 'number'` (line 89); when the token carries no `iat` claim the block at lines 91-101 is never executed, so `cacheValue[1]`/`cacheValue[2]` remain 0 and the `exp` claim is ignored. Line 106 then rewrites `cacheValue[2]` from 0 to `maxTTL` (= clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL, default 600000 ms), so the cached success entry is stored with min=0 and max=now+cacheTTL rather than the token's real `exp`. On subsequent verifications of the same token the cache-hit condition (lines 262-269) short-circuits on `min === 0` and accepts while `now <= max`, returning the previously validated payload without re-running verifyToken/validateClaimDateValue. An attacker holding a token that was issued without `iat` (a normal case) can therefore keep using it after its `exp` has passed — for up to the configured cacheTTL — obtaining an authorization bypass. Upstream fast-jwt 6.3.4 removed the `hasIat` gate and the `0 === no bound` sentinel, computing `expiresAt` from `exp`/`maxAge` unconditionally, confirming this version reintroduces expired-token acceptance.

review_queue.evidence: cacheSet derives the cached validity window only when a numeric iat exists, so cache:true keeps accepting a signed exp token without iat after expiry. round4-jwt-verification.json shows uncached and numeric-iat controls reject; cache opt-in is required.

finding.title: Unbounded Blake2b key length overflows fixed 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b(msg, key) and Blake2b.__init__ pass the caller's key straight to the C layer without any upper-bound check on len(key): line 281 calls crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) and line 297 calls crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key)). In monocypher.c crypto_blake2b_keyed_init (line 530) declares `u8 key_block[128] = {0};` and line 546 executes `COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` where COPY is a byte-copy loop (monocypher.c:65) of key_size bytes. BLAKE2 requires key_size <= 64, but nothing here enforces it, so any key longer than 128 bytes (e.g. blake2b(b'x', key=b'A'*300) or Blake2b(key=b'A'*300)) performs a stack-based out-of-bounds write of len(key)-128 bytes past key_block, corrupting the saved context/return address. The key is an attacker-reachable input whenever keyed hashing/verification uses key material derived from or supplied by a peer. Elligator/x25519 paths validate 32-byte lengths, showing the missing check is an oversight, not intended behavior.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: Unvalidated/nb_blocks-unchecked Argon2 work-area allocation yields heap overflow or NULL dereference
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 accepts nb_blocks with no validation: line 328 writes it to config.nb_blocks and line 345 allocates `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024))` without checking the return value before line 347 passes it to crypto_argon2. Monocypher expects nb_blocks to be a nonzero multiple of 4*lanes (>=8). With a small value such as nb_blocks=1, crypto_argon2 (monocypher.c:747) computes segment_size = nb_blocks/nb_lanes/4 = 0 and lane_size = 0, then unconditionally fills two full 1024-byte blocks via blocks[l*lane_size + i] for i in 0,1 (monocypher.c writes at blocks[0] and blocks[1]), i.e. 2048 bytes written into a 1024-byte allocation -> heap out-of-bounds write; last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1 also goes out of bounds. On 32-bit size_t the `<size_t> nb_blocks * 1024` product wraps (e.g. nb_blocks=0x400000 -> 0), turning attacker-controlled KDF parameters into an arbitrarily large heap overflow; on 64-bit it wraps in the C library usage or malloc returns NULL for very large nb_blocks and the unchecked pointer is dereferenced, aborting the process. nb_blocks/iteration counts commonly come from untrusted headers or PoW/KDF configuration, and the binding fails to enforce Monocypher's documented constraints.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: Missing fixed-length validation for signature/public_key/mac/nonce parameters causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: signature_check passes attacker-supplied buffers to a C routine that always reads 64+32 bytes without checking lengths: line 429 `crypto_eddsa_check(signature, public_key, message, len(message))`. If a peer supplies a signature shorter than 64 bytes or a public_key shorter than 32 bytes, crypto_eddsa_check/crypto_verify64 (monocypher.c) reads past the end of the Python bytes object, resulting in out-of-bounds reads and potential process crash during signature verification. The same omission exists in the module-level AEAD helpers: unlock (line 199) forwards mac and nonce without checking len(mac)==16/len(nonce)==24, and lock (line 181) forwards key/nonce without checking 32/24, whereas the IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption class does validate mac (line 246) and the constructor validates key/nonce (lines 214-218). compute_key_exchange_public_key (line 362) and key_exchange (line 375) likewise pass secret/public keys with no 32-byte check. The inconsistency with validated paths (elligator_map line 501, elligator_rev line 519) shows the checks are omitted rather than intentional.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear() double-drops elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: clear() runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` and only afterwards `self.set_len(0)`, with no panic guard. When any element's Drop unwinds, the slice drop glue has already dropped elements, but `set_len(0)` is skipped, so the header still reports the old length and the not-yet/ already-dropped slots are treated as live. The later `ThinVec::drop` (or a second clear) calls `drop_in_place` again over the same storage, dropping the same values a second time. For elements that own heap memory (Box/Rc/String/etc.) this is a double free / use-after-free class memory-corruption primitive. PoC executed under this build: push [E0, E1(panics on Drop), E2], call `v.clear()` inside `catch_unwind`; the drop counter shows E0 dropped once by clear, `v.len()` is still 3 after the panic, and `drop(v)` re-drops E0 (counter 1->2) plus all other elements, i.e. every element is dropped twice. A DropGuard setting len to 0 in a destructor (added upstream in 0.2.16) prevents it.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` -> `drop_non_singleton` moves the vector out (`mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())`), runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])`, and only then calls `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)`. If an element's Drop unwinds, `set_len_non_singleton(0)` never runs and the local `vec` is dropped during unwinding, invoking `ThinVec::drop` -> `drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the same buffer again, double-dropping the elements (double free for resource-owning elements). PoC executed under this build: a 3-element ThinVec where element 1 panics on Drop, consumed via `into_iter()` inside `catch_unwind`; the drop counter reports element 0 dropped twice immediately (drop0=2) as the `vec` local is re-dropped during unwind. Upstream fixed this in 0.2.16 by introducing a DropGuard that sets the length to 0 before the elements are dropped.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Bypassable index bound in ItemAtIndex lets a malicious prover force an out-of-range block selection and forge an all-zero SHA-256 output
finding.evidence: Attacker-controlled input flows into the array index without an effective bound. `paddedInLength` is a free prover input; sha.circom:110-111 derives `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` and constrains `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512`, and the only length guard (sha.circom:125-128, `LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits)` with `in[1] = maxBitLength`) allows `paddedInLength = 0`. With `paddedInLength = 0` the prover gets `inBlockIndex = 0`, so sha.circom:195 feeds `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1 = p-1` (i.e. -1) into `ItemAtIndex`. The sole check inside `ItemAtIndex` (array.circom:25-28) is `LessThan(bitLength)` with `lessThan.out === 1`. circomlib's `LessThan(n)` is implemented as `n2b.in <== in[0] + (1<<n) - in[1]; out <== 1 - n2b.out[n]` and never range-checks `in[0]`, so for `in[0] = p-1` the sum wraps to `2^n - maxArrayLen - 1 < 2^(n+1)`, bit n is 0 and the check returns 1: the out-of-range/negative index is accepted. Since array.circom:34-45 only sums `eqs[i].out * in[i]` and there is no constraint that exactly one index matches (the guard `calcTotalIndex.sum === 1` is absent), no `eqs[i]` fires and `out <== calcTotal.sum` becomes 0. Thus `sha.out` (sha.circom:196) and the wrapper's `out` are all zeros, letting the prover satisfy the circuit with a hash value that SHA-256 never produces for any input (a soundness/integrity break; e.g. any downstream check against an all-zero/default hash would accept the proof). The bounds check is insufficient because `LessThan` provides no canonical range check on its inputs, and `ItemAtIndex` relies on it alone.

review_queue.evidence: Sha256General/Sha256Partial derive inBlockIndex from an unbounded paddedInLength and feed inBlockIndex-1 into ItemAtIndex, whose LessThan lacks a range check. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.

finding.title: Unbounded Blake2b key length causes stack buffer overflow in monocypher
finding.evidence: Blake2b.__init__ (line 297) passes the caller-supplied `key` and its length straight to crypto_blake2b_keyed_init without any upper-bound check (the module-level blake2b() at line 281 and its call to crypto_blake2b_keyed have the identical flaw). Monocypher copies the key into a fixed 128-byte stack array with no bound: monocypher.c line 546 `COPY(key_block, key, key_size)` where `u8 key_block[128]`, and COPY is a plain element-wise loop (monocypher.c line 65 `#define COPY(dst, src, size) FOR(_i_, 0, size) (dst)[_i_] = (src)[_i_]`). Calling e.g. `Blake2b(key=bytes(200))` sets key_size=200 and writes 200 attacker-controlled bytes into the 128-byte stack buffer, overflowing adjacent stack memory. Cython performs no length validation for the `const uint8_t* key` parameter, so any `Blake2b(key=...)`/`blake2b(msg, key=...)` call with a key longer than 128 bytes reaches the unsafe COPY. CWE-121 (the Blake2b spec limit of 64 bytes is also not enforced).

review_queue.evidence: Blake2b.__init__ passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed_init, the same fixed key_block[128] copy as line 281. Genuine separate wrapper defect from the expected argon2 undersized work area.

finding.title: Missing length validation lets short cryptographic inputs cause out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: Several wrappers pass Python bytes objects directly as fixed-size C arrays without checking their length, so Cython forwards only the data pointer and Monocypher reads its fixed-size fields past the end of the Python buffer. signature_check (line 429) forwards attacker-controlled `signature`/`public_key` to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads 64-byte signature and 32-byte public_key; lock (line 181) passes `key`/`nonce` to crypto_aead_lock which reads key[32] and nonce[24]; unlock (line 199), chacha20 (lines 267/269), key_exchange (line 375) and compute_key_exchange_public_key (line 362) have the same defect (all read 32-byte key/nonce material). By contrast the module explicitly validates lengths in IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption, elligator_map/rev and the signing-key helpers, confirming the omission is unintentional. With e.g. `signature_check(b'X', b'Y', b'm')` or `lock(b'k', b'n', b'm')` the C code reads beyond the short heap buffers (out-of-bounds read), giving memory-safety/DoS and reading adjacent heap (potentially key material) into the verification/cipher math. CWE-125.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: Argon2 nb_blocks not validated against monocypher minimum, causing heap overflow
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 takes `nb_blocks` straight from the caller, allocates `malloc(nb_blocks * 1024)` (line 345) and calls crypto_argon2 (line 347) with config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks and nb_lanes = 1. monocypher.h line 160 documents the requirement `nb_blocks >= 8 * nb_lanes`, but the binding never enforces it. In monocypher.c crypto_argon2 the first-loop unconditionally fills two 1024-byte blocks per lane: `load64_le_buf(blocks[l * lane_size + i].a, hash_area, 128)` for i in {0,1}, i.e. blocks[0] and blocks[1]. With nb_blocks = 1 the work area is only 1024 bytes and lane_size becomes 0, so the second 1024-byte block write lands past the allocation: a heap buffer overflow of attacker-influenced length (nb_blocks = 0 additionally makes malloc(0) tiny/NULL). The value is caller-controlled, so a user-supplied nb_blocks below the documented minimum reaches a wild heap write. CWE-787.

review_queue.evidence: crypto_argon2 is called with the caller-sized work area; same undersized-work-area root cause as the expected line-345 sink.

finding.title: ChunkedReader discards chunk-footer bytes without validating CRLF, enabling HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
The audited target is h11 0.14.0 (h11/_version.py). Its ChunkedReader tracks the post-chunk footer with an integer count: line 197 sets `self._bytes_to_discard = 2`, and lines 163-170 (`data = buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard)` ... `self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)`) simply skip exactly two bytes without ever comparing them to b"
". The fixed upstream 0.16.0 code (diff of h11/_readers.py) instead stores the expected bytes `self._bytes_to_discard = b"
"` and raises `LocalProtocolError("malformed chunk footer ...")` when `data != self._bytes_to_discard[:len(data)]`; the audited 0.14.0 has no such check. Attacker flow: a client sends `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and terminates a chunk with two non-CRLF bytes (e.g. `5
AAAAA
X`); the reader accepts `
 X` as the chunk terminator and resumes de-framing, so bytes that a conforming parser would treat as body/footer are reinterpreted as the next chunk header. That desynchronizes h11 from an upstream/downstream hop that rejects or consumes the malformed footer differently, the classic request-smuggling primitive (CWE-444). Protections are insufficient because no validation of the trailing CRLF exists in the audited source; the only guard is the count reaching 0. Reachable via h11.Connection(SERVER/CLIENT).receive_data + next_event() on any chunked message. (Local reproduction attempt with the malformed footer timed out in this environment, so execution is claimed only at the source-diff level: the missing `data != self._bytes_to_discard` check present in the fixed release and absent here.)

review_queue.evidence: The chunked reader discards the footer/terminator bytes without CRLF validation. Same framing root cause as the expected line-197 sink.

finding.title: Unconstrained paddedInLength lets prover force all-zero SHA-256 output via out-of-range array selector index
finding.evidence: paddedInLength is an attacker-chosen field element (signal input at sha.circom:97 in Sha256General, :219 in Sha256Partial, :19 in Sha256Bytes). At line 110 the block count is derived with an unconstrained witness assignment `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9);` and the only relating constraint, line 111 `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;`, is a modular field equation that does not bound either value. The advertised range check on line 125-128 uses `bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits)` on the same unbounded `paddedInLength`; circomlib's LessThan (comparators.circom:89-99) is only sound when inputs fit n bits, so small negatives mod p (p-1, p-2, ...) are accepted as '< maxBitLength', exactly as flagged in the project's own zksecurity audit. The unvalidated value then flows to the selector sink: line 195 `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1;` inside the loop at lines 190-197. `inBlockIndex - 1` can therefore be a huge/negative field element (>= maxBlocks) that no IsEqual match in ItemAtIndex (array.circom:34-45) satisfies, so calcTotal.sum is the sum of all-zero terms and `arraySelectors[k].out` is 0 for every k, making `out[256]` the all-zero array independent of `paddedIn`. A malicious prover supplies paddedInLength in {0,-1,...,-64} (bytes variants scale it by 8 at line 33 / :65) and rewrites the witness-gen division `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength / 512)`, producing a valid proof that an arbitrary message hashes to 0. Sha256Partial is identically broken (lines 233-234, 237-240, and sink line 292) and both are reachable through Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial, so downstream consumers that verify a SHA-256 equality on attacker-influenced input accept forged openings.

review_queue.evidence: Missing lower bound on paddedInLength underflows the selector index. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.

finding.title: Unvalidated paddedInLength allows selector index underflow and forces a forged all-zero SHA256 output
finding.evidence: Attacker-controlled input is the signal `paddedInLength` (declared line 97, also reachable via `Sha256Bytes.paddedInLength` line 19/33 and `Sha256BytesPartial` line 50/65). It is assigned to `inBlockIndex` via `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` (line 110) and only related by `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111). That field equation is solvable for every `paddedInLength` (it merely defines `inBlockIndex = paddedInLength / 512` as a field element), and the only range check `bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits)` (lines 125-128) imposes an upper bound `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength`; there is no lower bound requiring `paddedInLength >= 512` nor any constraint that it be a multiple of 512. Consequently a prover can set `paddedInLength = 0`, giving `inBlockIndex = 0`; line 195 then computes `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1`, which underflows to the field element `p-1`. The `ItemAtIndex` range check `LessThan(bitLength); lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1` (array.circom lines 25-28) is unsound for an out-of-range field input: circomlib `LessThan` only decomposes `in[0] + 2^n - in[1]`, and for `index = p-1` this wraps mod p to a small in-range value, so the assert passes. No `eqs[i]` then matches `index`, so `CalculateTotal.sum` (array.circom lines 34-45) is 0 and every `out[k]` is forced to 0 (lines 195-196, and identically lines 292-293 in `Sha256Partial`). This is reachable by any prover with no secret: the circuit accepts a false statement and can be made to emit a constant `0x00..00` hash for inputs that have no valid SHA-256 preimage, breaking the hash binding that callers rely on. The same under-constraint lets every non-multiple-of-512 `paddedInLength` (e.g. 256) pass the `<= maxBitLength` check and also produce the forced zero output.

review_queue.evidence: paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512 follows the unbounded shift; same comparator/length root cause one line after the expected sink.
